item.title: Agent swarms have the potential to drive yet another leap in output from AI. The impact will be a clear separation between teams that adopt this pattern of work and those that don’t. The progression has roughly been: chat gave us quick turn AI responses that let us work a bit faster, but we were s...
item.description:
作者：Aaron Levie 账号：@levie 简介：ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
Agent swarms have the potential to drive yet another leap in output from AI. The impact will be a clear separation between teams that adopt this pattern of work and those that don’t.
The progression has roughly been: chat gave us quick turn AI responses that let us work a bit faster, but we were still rate limited by our interactions; then agents that can go off and complete entire tasks for us, accelerating hours or days of work into minutes; to now swarms of agents that are goal seeking and will find any route to the successful completion of a project, where there’s no inherent limit to the productivity gains.
We can imagine a future where, for any task in which value can be created within a self-contained digital environment, swarms will be able to complete the work faster than any other approach.
Essentially any area where value creation is currently bound by the amount of research you can do, the amount of decisions made with a set of software tools, the amount of data processed or consumed, and the amount of code (or code adjacent) that can be generated.
This means swarms will play a big role in game development, coding, trading, life sciences research, IT automation, cyber, math breakthroughs, animation, and plenty of other areas of work that have these characteristics.
There’s a lot of opportunity to build the harnesses, applied AI products, and infrastructure for how these agents operate. And most importantly there’s a ton of opportunity for those that can wire up work in this way. It’s going to be an entire new field of FDE work available.

item.description:
作者：Aaron Levie 账号：@levie 简介：ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
Agents are going to work with enterprise files 100X more than people do today. This is why we're excited to partner with Anthropic to bring full read/write interoperability to Box content via Claude.
Now you can have an agent not only pull up content to work with in a workflow, but also write back file updates to Box and view them directly inside of Claude, all via MCP. You can create, edit, and update contracts, presentations, strategy docs, and any other content.
When we started Box we couldn't have imagined all the ways that we'd be working with our unstructured data in the future, but it's clear that agents and people will be producing vastly more artifacts than we imagined. We're building the platform that makes it incredibly seamless and secure to work with your content from any agent.

item.title: Designing for Agents — Zeno Rocha, Resend
item.description:
播客：Latent Space
It's like, oh my gosh, how are we ever gonna beat SendGrid? It's im- just impossible.
And then earlier this year, we crossed a number of, uh, downloads from SendGrid, and I was like, "That's insane," and now we're more than double.
So Resend now is powering four point three million users as of this morning. Uh, we have all sorts of customers like, uh, Warner Brothers, HBO. There was a Japanese gang that recently came.
They, they brought like maybe twenty thousand domains at Resend. Like, those are twenty thousand different TLDs registered in different domain registrars, and we are a ten million AR company.
I would rather live in that reality than live in a reality where we're a hundred million dollar company and my daughter doesn't wanna play with me, is not interested in me, and we're, we're not that close.
So we are-- we're building the infrastructure and going, like, down to the metal now. But it's a big project. Like, we've been working for months now, and we're gonna announce something soon about that.
[upbeat music] Okay, we're in the studio with Zino Rocha. Rocha? Rocha. Rocha from Resend. Uh, you and I go back to your VS Code theme days- Yes. [laughs]... when you're just an indie hacker. Yeah.
And I was like, "Man, uh, I don't know what this guy does, but everything he does has taste." And then now you made, built an email infrastructure platform. Uh, anyway, welcome. You undersell just a indie hacker.
[laughs] Top twenty most active GitHub under twenty twenty, '22. [laughs] Nice. Right. Very, very active open source stuff. Yeah, yeah. What's your typical how do you introduce yourself these days?
Yeah, I think I just focus on my recent career. For the longest time, uh, even today when I say like, "Oh, I created Dracula," people know Dracula more than Resend, but, uh- Still. Yeah, but it's been nice.
Like, there's a... Uh, yeah, it's changing. [laughs] Yeah. What was the impetus for, I guess, picking email? You know, I think, uh, you know, uh, people always have, like, obviously React email and all those things.
Yeah. [sighs] I just don't know if I would have made it a company, you know? Yeah. If, if I knew, like, how hard email is, I, I probably wouldn't start the company either. Uh- Yeah.
Were, were you a primarily JavaScript front-end- Totally... CSS dev- I was a front-end guy. No infra, right? No email background. The HTML5 guy- Right... you know?
And I think what was interesting and what drew me to it is like I just look at all the tools, uh, around that, and I've used all of them before, the MailGuns, the MailChimps, the SendGrids of the world, and I've always felt like, man, there should be something where, um, there's just some- someone should care about this space.
That's, that, that's how I felt. Like, you have all these players. It's a massive market, a lot of competitors, but no one that cares about the developer persona.
Maybe they care about the marketer, the product manager or whatever, but not for the developer. So I started just building around that premise of like, if this was the, the Stripe of email, how would that look like?
Um, and yeah, the, like I had no idea or knew nothing about email. Like I was a user of email, but I have never built like an email pipeline and, and all that- Yeah... infrastructure before.
Yeah, I mean, like, you know, typically if you ask me, like Postmark was still a thing. Yeah. But like, uh, and then, and then obviously SendGrid and all these folks- Mm-hmm...
all these guys, and they're still around, but like, uh, they're not, uh, maybe as innovative as someone who's like a new YC startup, like trying to, try to make it. Yeah. Um, just to, just upfront- Mm-hmm...
I like to let people brag a bit. Mm-hmm. And you-- Like for people who never heard of Resend, what are like- Yeah... the, the ways that you talk about, like the most impressive numbers, the logos, anything? Yeah.
So Resend now is powering four point three million users as of this morning.
Uh, we have all sorts of customers like, uh, Warner Brothers, HBO, so customers that are really big and have all sorts of demands, but also a lot of indie hackers and folks who are just building a website, building their own application.
And yeah, we just crossed a hundred and twenty thousand paid customers and yeah. Like the endless logo wall. [laughs] Oh my God. Yeah, the big logo wall. Do you think this is effective? Yeah. You wanted the flex.
There you, there you go. You know what? Like in the beginning, I felt like I just need to have some sort of social proof. Uh-huh. [laughs] And then in the end I was like, "You know what? This is actually pretty cool."
And I, I, I honestly, like, I found companies like Warner Brothers just like on a random Saturday.
Uh, I was just-- This was before AI, so I, I'll go to my database, I'm like, "Oh, let me see who can I put on the website?" And I just... I did the, the most naive thing you can do.
Like, let me look at the domains- Yeah... and let me just filter by dot coms and filter by the small ones. And there was this domain, WBD, Warner Brothers Discovery. I didn't know. What is wbd.com?
[laughs] And I was like, "Oh, no. Warner Brothers is using us." So yeah, I j- I, I just love fe-featuring customers and yeah. [laughs] Pretty good. Specifically for listeners- Mm-hmm...
one of the reasons I reached out for this interview, one, you know, I'm, uh, I, I should declare upfront, I'm, I am an angel. Mm-hmm. Uh, when you sent me the memo, it was- Mm-hmm... super simple.
You were like, "Look, uh, MailChimp has exited. Postmark has exited. SendGrid is under Twilio. Who is doing this?" Yeah. And I was like, "Okay, yeah. Seems, seems right." [laughs] Yeah.
[laughs] No, honestly, like in terms of like the, the pitches I get- Mm-hmm... I've invested in about like thirty-plus companies. Mm-hmm. That was like one of the most straightforward things ever. [laughs] Oh.
[laughs] And then, uh, secondly, I, yeah, I don't like to add API keys. Yeah. Right? Like I like to have everything on one platform, one AP- one API key, copy everything. So- Yeah... uh, Cloudflare has built-in email.
Yep. And I had a project, and I set up my Cloudflare email domain- Mm-hmm... DNS, all that junk, uh, D- Yep... DKIM- Yeah... what have you, right? I don't know all the alphabet soup of stuff. Yeah.
And I already had this set up, and then I was like, "Okay, well, I wanna add another sort of email thing." Mm-hmm. Bloody model s- said, "You must add Resend."
[laughs] And I'm like, "Who the fuck is telling me this, uh, Resend, that like, you know, even already I, I have a Cloudflare email set up, and it's just still recommending it." It's on the, on the screen now.
This is him praising- Yeah. [laughs]... and like, "I don't need Resend, but you want me to keep adding Resend." Yeah. So okay, who did you bribe in OpenAI and Anthropic to get Resend on there?
[laughs] Oh, man, I, I wish there was someone to bribe because, yeah, I would definitely be paying them. [laughs]But I do personally spend a lot of time on, on that topic.
Like, that's something that I feel like every generation, that-that's why I was so interested to build this thing in the first place. Yeah. Like, every generation, you have those tools that define that moment, right?
We remember the Heroku days. I mean, Netlify Purcell. You know? Yeah.
And, and so to me it was like, yeah, there's room for a new generation, and this new generation is not gonna be distributed in the same places that it was before.
So since the beginning I was, like, very focused on, okay, we, we gotta be number one when someone asks about that. Yeah. You're very number one, CloudCode recommending 60% plus of the time.
I think it'll be fun to see the playbook, how do you, how do you win that? Um, I do wanna get back into, okay, so you said you had no idea why email, how to start email. Yeah.
I think a lot of people actually don't understand what goes into making a service like t...

We’ve been testing it at @every across coding, writing, design, and knowledge work. It can work for hours on an ambitious project, but it doesn’t always know when to stop...
item.description:
作者：Dan Shipper 账号：@danshipper 简介：ceo @every | the only subscription you need to stay at the edge of AI
BREAKING:
@Google just dropped Gemini 4 Carbon. It’s a much better coder than Argon—but I’m probably keeping Argon for writing.
We’ve been testing it at @every across coding, writing, design, and knowledge work. It can work for hours on an ambitious project, but it doesn’t always know when to stop.
Here’s your day-zero vibe check:
• Coding: On one run of our Senior Engineer benchmark, Carbon scored 44%, versus Argon’s 21%. A big improvement, though still middle of the pack. In a separate test, @hammer_mt gave it a backlog to work through. It identified 6 tasks as ready, then did 15—including work someone else was already doing. He stopped it after almost 4.5 hours.
• Big builds: @RandyCounsman gave it 3D scans of our podcast studio and an equipment list. In one attempt, it built a browser-based model accurate enough to check whether new gear would fit without getting into the shot. He estimates Carbon also wrote about 95% of a big update to Everycut, our internal video editor.
• Code quality: @kieranklaassen values its tests and documentation on large projects, including its record of approaches it considered and rejected. Fable remains his first choice, but Carbon has earned a place alongside it. The catch: It can produce huge files where Fable keeps things more modular.
• Audio and video: Randy found it caught audio editing issues other models missed. Kieran handed it a recorded meeting and asked for shorts. It came back with 6 titled clips.
• Design: @jackcheng got a hyperrealistic ginkgo-leaf app icon with details other models struggle with. Objects and 3D scenes look better than Argon’s. Interfaces split the team: Jack and Randy kept getting boxes within boxes, while @TylerNishida liked its ideas for new interfaces. Kieran says giving it design guidance makes a big difference.
• Writing: Our editorial benchmark put Carbon and Argon about even. If you like Argon, you’ll probably like Carbon. But Carbon costs more, and I haven’t seen enough improvement to justify switching.
My Reach Test: 🟨 I’ll use it sometimes.
Give it one big job with a clear finish line, and review what comes back. It’s also worth trying as a second opinion, especially on audio and video.
Full vibe check coming soon: https://t.co/Ch2pNl9Po5

Don't wait until it's done or perfect. Share a work in progress. Sometimes that's how you figure out if it's even worth finishing.
